SeeDeuteronomy 6:16, footnotea. This Hebrew word is different from the word used inMalachi 3:10, which contains the Lord’s invitation to “prove me now” through the payment of tithes. While the Hebrew word for “prove” inMalachi 3:10can also mean “to test,” its use in this verse presents a positive way the Lord invites us to test Him—by acting in faith to receive His promised blessings (see Longman and Strauss,The Baker Expository Dictionary, “Test,” 818).

This pattern includes: (1) preamble (Deuteronomy 1:6); (2) historical prologue (Deuteronomy 1–4); (3) stipulations (Deuteronomy 5–26); (4) blessings and curses (Deuteronomy 27–28); (5) witnesses (Deuteronomy 30–31); (6) provisions for depositing the text and for public reading (Deuteronomy 31–32); and (7) covenant ceremonies (Deuteronomy 29–30) (see Richard Neitzel Holzapfel and others,Jehovah and the World of the Old Testament: An Illustrated Reference for Latter-day Saints[2009], 138–42).

See Longman and Strauss,The Baker Expository Dictionary, entry 8085, page 1028. For Jews, the Shema is more than a prayer. It is a pledge of commitment to God and a renewal of the oaths that the children of Israel made at Mount Sinai (see Adele Berlin and Marc Zvi Brettler, eds.,The Jewish Study Bible, 2nd ed. [2014], 339). “The meaning of the phrase ‘the Lord our God is one Lord,’ can be best appreciated by comparing a different translation: ‘The Lord is our God, the Lord alone’ [New Jewish Publication Society of America Tanakh]. This ‘confession of faith’ … defines the covenantal relationship between God and his people—he is ‘our God’—and it acknowledges the oneness and exclusiveness of Jehovah” (Holzapfel and others,Jehovah and the World of the Old Testament, 139).
